pl-l3d29c2-d1e115.summary: Notes that this question is often raised and made difficult by the saints' varied statements.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e118.summary: Reports a view that all are to be loved with equal affection, with distinction only in effect, that is, in the services shown.
claims: Some hold that all are loved with equal affection but served unequally.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e121.summary: Quotes Augustine: all men are to be loved equally, but since you cannot benefit all, you must provide especially for those joined to you more closely by place, time, or circumstance, as by a kind of lot.
claims: All men are loved equally, but help goes first to those more closely joined to us.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e131.summary: Quotes Augustine on Galatians: do good to all, especially to the household of faith; eternal life is to be wished for all with equal love, though not all can be shown the same services, which are owed especially to brothers, members of one another with the same Father.
claims: Eternal life is to be wished for all with equal love.
Services are owed especially to fellow Christians.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e143.summary: States that on these and other testimonies some rely in saying all are to be loved equally by affection of charity, with difference in the exhibition of works.
claims: Some hold equal affection with unequal works.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e146.summary: Objects with the commandment to honor father and mother: why command this specially of parents unless they are to be loved more?
claims: The commandment to honor parents suggests greater love for them.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e155.summary: Reports their reply: this refers to outward exhibition, in which parents come first; hence it says 'honor', not 'love'.
claims: Honoring parents concerns outward exhibition, not affection.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e161.summary: Objects with Jerome on Ezekiel: by the order of charity, after God the Father of all, one's father, mother, son, daughter, brother, and sister are to be loved.
claims: Jerome teaches an order of charity in love of kin.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e176.summary: Adds Ambrose on 'he set charity in order in me': many have disordered charity, putting first what is third or fourth. God is to be loved first, then parents, then children, then household, the good of whom are preferred to bad children. So the Gospel assigns to each its own: God with all strength, neighbor as oneself, enemies simply, not with all strength nor as oneself; it suffices that we love and do not hate them.
claims: Ambrose orders love: God, parents, children, household.
Enemies are commanded to be loved simply.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e195.summary: Draws out that these authorities plainly suggest a distinction in the affection of charity: men are to be loved with different, not equal, affection: God first, ourselves second, parents third, then children and siblings, then household, finally enemies.
claims: The authorities suggest an order in affection: God, self, parents, children and siblings, household, enemies.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e198.summary: Reports the opponents' reply: the order described refers to exhibition of works, shown differently to parents, children, household, and enemies; God alone is to be loved first in affection and service.
claims: Opponents refer the order to works, except for God.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e201.summary: Adds that some of them teach that neighbors are to be loved by the affection of charity as much as we love ourselves.
claims: Some hold that neighbors are loved as much as ourselves.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e204.summary: Gives their support from Augustine: incomparably more charity is owed to God than to ourselves, and to the brother as much as to ourselves; and we love ourselves the more, the more we love God.
claims: Augustine says the brother is owed as much charity as ourselves.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e210.summary: States their conclusion: all men are to be loved equally and as much as ourselves, God more, and our body less; the list of four objects gives only what is to be loved, not an order.
claims: Opponents hold all men loved equally and as much as ourselves.
They deny that the list of four objects gives an order.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e213.summary: States the alternative: since Ambrose's words, carefully examined, explain the order of love more in affection than in effect, others say, not unlearnedly, that a different order holds not only in works but also in affection: God, ourselves, parents, children or siblings, household, enemies.
claims: The order of charity holds in affection as well as in works.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e217.summary: Interprets Augustine's 'all are to be loved equally' as referring not to affection but to the good wished: we should wish all to merit equal goods, as Paul wished all to be as he was, the lesser attaining the perfection of the greater; or 'equal love' means the same love.
claims: Augustine's equality refers to the good wished, not to affection.
'Equal love' can mean the same charity.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e229.summary: Begins the interpretation of Augustine's saying that we should love brothers as much as ourselves (sentence continues).

pl-l3d29c2-d1e235.summary: Continues: it can be understood thus, that we love brothers for as great a good (sentence continues).

pl-l3d29c2-d1e238.summary: Completes the interpretation: as for ourselves, wishing them as great an eternal good as ourselves, though not with as great affection; or 'as much' expresses likeness, not quantity.
claims: We should wish brothers as great an eternal good as ourselves, not with equal affection.
'As much' can express likeness, not quantity.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e244.summary: Raises another question: if our parents, children, or siblings are wicked, are they to be loved more or less than good people not related to us?

pl-l3d29c2-d1e247.summary: Begins the answer: it seems that good people not joined to us by flesh (sentence continues).

pl-l3d29c2-d1e251.summary: Continues: are to be loved more than the wicked joined by flesh, because they are (sentence continues).

pl-l3d29c2-d1e254.summary: Completes the reasoning: they are joined to us in heart by the glue of charity, and the bond of hearts is holier than that of bodies.
claims: Good strangers seem more to be loved than wicked kin.
The bond of hearts is holier than that of bodies.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e257.summary: Confirms with Bede on 'my mother and my brothers are those who do the word of God': Christ does not wrongly neglect his mother, whom he acknowledges from the cross, but shows that the bonds of minds are more religious than those of bodies.
claims: Bonds of mind are more religious than bonds of body.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e269.summary: Admits that this question is obscure and cannot be fully resolved here, since he hurries on to other things.
claims: The question of good strangers and wicked kin remains unresolved.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e272.summary: Raises a difficulty from the saying (from Ambrose) that enemies are commanded to be loved not with all strength nor as oneself, but simply, since it suffices that we love and do not hate them.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e278.summary: Interprets it: it does not mean that it suffices to love an enemy and not as oneself, since all, friends and enemies, are to be loved as oneself. The Lord shows degrees: God with all strength, neighbor as oneself (not with all strength, showing he is loved less than God), enemies simply. 'It suffices that we love and do not hate' means it suffices to say this, not that we need not love them as ourselves, for they are neighbors; but it suffices if we love them less than other neighbors.
claims: Enemies are to be loved as ourselves, since they are neighbors.
Enemies may be loved less than other neighbors.
The Gospel's wording shows degrees of love.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e297.summary: Asks why the Lord commands love of enemies when elsewhere he commands hating parents and children.

pl-l3d29c2-d1e303.summary: Answers that two things are to be loved in a man, nature and virtue, and vice and sin are to be hated. So parents are to be hated insofar as they are wicked, and enemies loved insofar as they are men. Let us love enemies to be won for God's kingdom, hate in kin what hinders from it, and love in all the nature God made.
claims: Nature and virtue are to be loved in a man; vice and sin hated.
Kin are to be hated insofar as they hinder from God's kingdom.
Enemies are loved as men to be won for the kingdom.

pl-l3d29c2.summary: Examines a question made difficult by the saints' varied statements: must all men be loved with equal affection? Some, relying on Augustine, hold that all are to be loved with equal affection of charity, with distinction only in the effect, the services shown; some add that the neighbor is to be loved as much as ourselves. Against them stand the commandment to honor parents, Jerome, and especially Ambrose, who orders love: God, parents, children, household, and enemies simply. Lombard reports, as not unlearned, the view that the order holds in affection as well as in effect: God, self, parents, children and siblings, household, enemies; Augustine's equality refers to the good wished, equal beatitude, or to the same love. Whether good strangers are to be loved more than wicked kin is left an obscure question, though Bede favors the bond of hearts. Enemies are to be loved as ourselves, though less than other neighbors; and we love the nature in all and hate the vice even in kin.
claims: Some hold that all are loved with equal affection and differ only in services shown.
Ambrose and Jerome teach an order of charity in affection.
Lombard favors an order in affection as well as effect: God, self, parents, children, household, enemies.
Augustine's 'equal love' refers to the good wished or to the same love.
Enemies are to be loved as ourselves, but may be loved less than other neighbors.
We are to love nature in all and hate sin even in kin.
